slides.narration: A grain of pollen or a red blood cell is far too small to see in detail with the eye alone. Optical instruments do not make objects bigger; they make them look bigger by increasing the angle they subtend at the eye. In this part we work out how much a single convex lens can do, and how two lenses together form a compound microscope.

slides.heading: Angular size and magnifying power
slides.body_md:
How big an object **looks** depends on the angle it subtends at the eye. The eye cannot focus closer than the **near point**, the least distance of distinct vision, $D = 25$ cm. The **magnifying power** of an instrument is
$$M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{\text{angle subtended at the eye by the final image}}{\text{angle subtended by the object without the instrument}}$$
bullets: For a microscope, α is the angle when the object is held at D, the closest the unaided eye can view it clearly.
For small angles, an angle is (height)/(distance).

rows: Object held at D = 25 cm from the eye
Object at its actual (very large) distance

visual.alt: Table defining the two angles in the magnifying power beta over alpha: for a microscope, alpha is the angle of the object held at 25 centimetres; for a telescope, the angle of the object where it is; beta is always the angle of the final image at the eye

slides.narration: An object looks larger when it subtends a larger angle at the eye. Bringing it closer helps, but only down to the near point, about twenty five centimetres, where the eye can still focus. So we compare two angles: beta, the angle of the final image seen through the instrument, and alpha, the angle of the object viewed as well as possible without it. Their ratio is the magnifying power.

slides.heading: Simple microscope: image at D
slides.body_md:
Hold a convex lens close to the eye with the object **inside F**. The image is virtual, erect and enlarged; put it at D: $v = -D$. With the eye at the lens, $\beta = \dfrac{h}{|u|}$ and $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{D}$, so $M = \dfrac{D}{|u|}$.
From $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$ with $v = -D$: $\dfrac{1}{|u|} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{D}$, hence
$$M = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}$$

slides.narration: Place the object inside the focus of a convex lens held close to the eye. The lens forms a virtual, erect, enlarged image, and we adjust it to lie at the near point. The object subtends an angle h over u at the eye, compared with h over D when held at the near point without the lens. Using the lens formula with v equal to minus D, the ratio becomes one plus D over f.

slides.heading: Simple microscope: image at infinity
slides.body_md:
For a **relaxed eye**, put the object **at F**: the rays leave the lens parallel and the image is at infinity. Now $\beta = \dfrac{h}{f}$ and still $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{D}$, so
$$M = \dfrac{D}{f}$$
bullets: This is one less than with the image at D, but the eye can view it for a long time without strain.
In both cases a lens of shorter focal length magnifies more.

slides.narration: Viewing an image at the near point strains the eye. If the object is moved out to the focus, the rays leave the lens parallel and the relaxed eye sees the image at infinity. The object then subtends h over f at the lens, and the magnifying power is D over f, one less than before. Either way, a lens with a shorter focal length gives a larger magnifying power.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a reading magnifier
slides.body_md: A reading magnifier is a convex lens of focal length 12.5 cm. Find (a) where the print must be held for the image to form at D = 25 cm, (b) the magnifying power then, (c) the magnifying power with the image at infinity.
bullets: (a) $\dfrac{1}{|u|} = \dfrac{1}{12.5} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{3}{25}$, so the print is 8.33 cm from the lens.
(b) $M = 1 + \dfrac{25}{12.5} = 3$ (also the linear magnification $v/u = 25/8.33$).
(c) Print at F, 12.5 cm away: $M = \dfrac{25}{12.5} = 2$.

slides.narration: For the image at the near point, one over u is one over twelve and a half plus one over twenty five, which is three over twenty five, so the print is about eight point three centimetres from the lens. The magnifying power is one plus twenty five over twelve and a half, which is three. With the print at the focus and a relaxed eye it is two.

slides.heading: Why a single lens is not enough
slides.body_md: To magnify more, a simple microscope needs a shorter focal length. But a lens of focal length a few millimetres is tiny and strongly curved: the object must be almost touching it, the field of view is small, and the image is blurred and coloured by **aberrations**.
bullets: In practice a simple microscope gives M up to about 10.
For more, use two lenses: a compound microscope.

slides.narration: The graph shows that the magnifying power rises steeply as the focal length gets shorter. So why not use a lens of a few millimetres? Such a lens is tiny and very curved, the object almost touches it, and the image suffers from blurring and coloured fringes. Simple magnifiers therefore stop at about ten times. For more, we use two lenses one after the other.

slides.heading: The compound microscope
slides.body_md: The **objective** (short focal length $f_o$, small aperture) faces the object, placed **just beyond $F_o$**. It forms a **real, inverted, enlarged** image A′B′ inside the tube. The **eyepiece** (focal length $f_e$) acts as a simple microscope on A′B′, which lies **inside $F_e$**, and forms a large **virtual** final image A″B″ at D.
bullets: The final image is inverted with respect to the object.
The diagram is drawn to scale along the axis; only the heights are enlarged.

slides.narration: A compound microscope has two converging lenses. The objective, of very short focal length, is placed so that the object sits just beyond its focus. It forms a real, inverted and enlarged image inside the tube. The eyepiece is set so that this image lies just inside its own focus; it acts as a magnifying glass and forms a large virtual image at the near point. The final image is upside down.

slides.heading: Magnifying power with the final image at D
slides.body_md:
Let A′B′ have height $h'$ and be $|u_e|$ from the eyepiece. The final image subtends $\beta = \dfrac{h'}{|u_e|}$ at the eye; the object at D would subtend $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{D}$. So
$$M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{h'}{h}\cdot\dfrac{D}{|u_e|} = m_o\, m_e,\qquad m_o = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|},\quad m_e = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}$$
$$M = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right) \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$$
bullets: Approximation: the object is close to $F_o$ ($|u_o| \approx f_o$) and $v_o \approx L$, the distance of A′B′ from the objective (about the tube length).

For a relaxed eye, the eyepiece is moved out until A′B′ lies **at $F_e$**; the final image is at infinity:

bullets: The ISC syllabus asks for this expression only; its derivation is not required.
Worked example 2 set this way: M = 5 × 25/6.25 = 20, lenses 15.25 cm apart.

slides.narration: Most people use a microscope with a relaxed eye. The eyepiece is then moved out until the first image sits exactly at its focus, so the rays leave parallel and the final image is at infinity. The eyepiece factor becomes D over f e instead of one plus D over f e. You need to know this expression, but not its derivation. For our example the power drops from twenty five to twenty.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a laboratory microscope
slides.body_md: A laboratory microscope has an objective of focal length 0.60 cm, which forms its image 18 cm from it, and an eyepiece of focal length 2.0 cm. Find the magnifying power (a) with the final image at D, (b) at infinity. Compare with the estimate L/f_o.
bullets: Objective: $m_o = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|} = \dfrac{v_o}{f_o} - 1 = 30 - 1 = 29$ (the object is 0.621 cm away).
Estimate with $L/f_o = 30$: $M \approx 405$ at D, about 3% high.

visual.alt: Table comparing the compound microscope with the final image at D and at infinity: exact and approximate magnifying power, lens separation, and the values for the worked example

slides.narration: From the lens formula, the objective’s magnification is v o over f o minus one, which here is twenty nine. With the final image at the near point the eyepiece contributes thirteen and a half, giving a magnifying power of about three hundred and ninety. With a relaxed eye it contributes twelve and a half, giving about three hundred and sixty. The quick estimate L over f o gives thirty instead of twenty nine, a few per cent high.

slides.heading: Choosing the lenses
slides.body_md: Since $M \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$, a powerful microscope needs:
bullets: An objective of **very short** $f_o$ (a few millimetres): a large real image of an object just beyond $F_o$.
An eyepiece of **short** $f_e$: a strong magnifier for that image.
A longer tube helps too, but tubes are kept to about 16–20 cm for convenience.
Placing the object at 2F would give m_o = 1: no gain from the objective.

rows: Image moved from D to infinity
Smaller by a factor D/(f_e + D)

visual.alt: Table of how shorter focal lengths, a longer tube and moving the final image to infinity change the magnifying power of a compound microscope

slides.narration: The formula tells us how to design a microscope. The objective should have a very short focal length, so that an object just beyond its focus gives a large real image far down the tube. The eyepiece should also have a short focal length, so that it magnifies that image strongly. If the object were placed at twice the focal length, the objective would not magnify at all.

slides.narration: To sum up: magnifying power is the ratio of the angle subtended by the final image to the angle subtended by the object at the near point. A simple microscope gives one plus D over f with the image at D, and D over f with the image at infinity. A compound microscope multiplies the objective’s linear magnification by the eyepiece’s magnifying power.

slides.narration: The Moon’s craters and Saturn’s rings are huge, but so far away that they subtend tiny angles. A telescope increases those angles. In this part we study the refracting astronomical telescope, the mirror telescopes used by large observatories, and then a different question: not how much a microscope magnifies, but how fine a detail it can actually separate.

slides.heading: The refracting astronomical telescope
slides.body_md: Two converging lenses on a common axis:
bullets: **Objective:** long focal length $f_o$ and **large aperture**, to collect plenty of light from the distant object and form a real image at its focus.
**Eyepiece:** short focal length $f_e$, a magnifier for that image.
The object cannot be brought closer, so α is the angle it subtends where it is (practically, at the objective or the eye).

rows: Collects light, forms a real image at F_o

visual.alt: Table comparing the objective and the eyepiece of a refracting telescope: focal length, aperture and job

slides.narration: An astronomical telescope also uses two converging lenses, but the roles are reversed compared with a microscope. The objective has a long focal length and a wide aperture, to gather as much light as possible and form a real image of the distant object at its focus. The eyepiece has a short focal length and magnifies that image. Because we cannot bring a star closer, alpha is simply the angle it subtends where it is.

slides.heading: Normal adjustment: image at infinity
slides.body_md:
Rays from the top of a distant object arrive parallel at angle α. The objective focuses them to I in its focal plane, a height $h$ below the axis: $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{f_o}$. In **normal adjustment** I is also at the focus of the eyepiece, so the rays leave parallel at angle $\beta = \dfrac{h}{f_e}$:
$$M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e},\qquad L = f_o + f_e$$
bullets: The final image is at infinity and inverted.

slides.narration: Rays from the top of a distant object reach the objective parallel to one another, at a small angle alpha. The objective brings them to a point in its focal plane, at a height h equal to f o times alpha. In normal adjustment that point is also at the focus of the eyepiece, so the rays leave parallel at angle beta equal to h over f e. The ratio is f o over f e, and the lenses are f o plus f e apart.

slides.heading: Final image at D
slides.body_md:
Push the eyepiece in until I is a distance $|u_e|$ inside its focus, with the final image at D: $\dfrac{1}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{1}{f_e} + \dfrac{1}{D}$. Now $\beta = \dfrac{h}{|u_e|}$ and $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{f_o}$:
$$M = \dfrac{f_o}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_e}{D}\right),\qquad L = f_o + |u_e|$$
bullets: Larger M than in normal adjustment, slightly shorter tube, but a strained eye.

slides.heading: Inverted images, brightness and size
slides.body_md: An astronomical telescope gives an **inverted** image. That does not matter for stars and planets; terrestrial telescopes and binoculars add an erecting lens or prisms.
bullets: A wider objective collects more light (in proportion to its area), so faint objects look brighter and finer detail is resolved; M depends only on the focal lengths.
Large lenses are heavy, sag, absorb light and show colour fringes: very large telescopes use mirrors.

visual.alt: Table of how the light collected grows with the square of the objective diameter: doubling the diameter collects four times as much light

slides.narration: The image in an astronomical telescope is upside down, which does not matter for the sky; telescopes for use on land add an extra lens or prisms to turn it the right way up. The width of the objective does not change the magnifying power, but it matters a great deal: the light collected grows with its area, so a wider objective shows fainter objects and finer detail.

slides.heading: The Cassegrain reflecting telescope
slides.body_md: A large **concave paraboloidal primary mirror** collects the light and reflects it towards its focus. A small **convex secondary mirror** inside that focus sends it back through a **hole** in the primary to a focus F behind it, where the **eyepiece** (or a camera) is placed. With the image at infinity, $M = \dfrac{F}{f_e}$, where F is the focal length of the mirror system.
bullets: The convex secondary also spreads the cone, so F is several times the focal length of the primary in a short tube.
India’s 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope near Nainital uses a Cassegrain-type mirror design.

slides.narration: Large telescopes use mirrors. In the Cassegrain design, a big concave mirror shaped as a paraboloid collects the light and sends it towards its focus. Before it gets there, a small convex mirror sends it back through a hole in the centre of the big mirror, to a focus just behind it, where the eyepiece or camera sits. The secondary also makes the system behave like a much longer focus objective, packed into a short tube.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a Cassegrain telescope
slides.body_md: The primary mirror of a small Cassegrain telescope has a focal length of 60 cm. A convex secondary of focal length 20 cm is 45 cm in front of it. Find where the final focus forms, the focal length of the mirror system, and M with an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm (image at infinity).
bullets: The primary alone would focus 60 cm away, 15 cm beyond the secondary: a virtual object for it. Mirror formula: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{1}{60}$, $v = 60$ cm: the focus is 15 cm **behind** the primary.
The secondary enlarges the image $\dfrac{60}{15} = 4$ times, so $F = 4 \times 60 = 240$ cm (in a tube under 60 cm long).
$M = \dfrac{F}{f_e} = \dfrac{240}{4.0} = 60$; the eyepiece is 4.0 cm beyond the focus.

slides.narration: The primary on its own would bring the light to a focus sixty centimetres away, fifteen centimetres beyond the secondary. For the convex secondary this is a virtual object, and the mirror formula puts the new focus sixty centimetres from it, fifteen centimetres behind the primary. The image is four times larger, so the system acts like a single objective of two hundred and forty centimetres, and a four centimetre eyepiece gives sixty.

slides.heading: Why mirrors? Chromatic and spherical aberration
slides.body_md: The refractive index of glass depends on colour, so a lens focuses blue light nearer than red: **chromatic aberration** (coloured fringes). The law of reflection does not involve n, so a mirror brings every colour to the same focus.
bullets: A spherical mirror of large aperture focuses edge rays short of the paraxial focus (**spherical aberration**); a **paraboloidal** mirror brings all parallel rays to one point.

slides.narration: Glass bends blue light more than red, so a lens brings the colours to slightly different foci and bright objects show coloured fringes. Reflection does not depend on the refractive index at all, so a mirror focuses every colour at the same point. A spherical mirror still focuses its outer rays a little short of the centre ones, but a mirror ground to a paraboloid brings a whole parallel beam to a single point.

slides.heading: Advantages of reflecting telescopes
slides.body_md: Compared with a refractor of the same aperture, a reflecting telescope:
bullets: Has **no chromatic aberration**, and no spherical aberration with a paraboloidal mirror.
Can be made **much larger**: a mirror is supported over its whole back, while a lens can be held only at its edge and sags.
Needs only **one surface** figured and no flawless glass; it absorbs no light in the glass, so it is cheaper and brighter.
Collects more light and so shows fainter objects and **resolves finer detail**; the Cassegrain folding gives a **short tube**.

slides.narration: Mirrors win for large telescopes. They have no colour fringes, and a paraboloid has no spherical aberration either. A mirror can be supported over its entire back, while a lens can only be held at its rim and sags under its own weight. Only one surface has to be shaped, the glass need not be flawless, and no light is lost passing through it. The large aperture shows fainter objects, and the folded design keeps the tube short.

slides.heading: Resolving power of a microscope
slides.body_md:
Magnifying an image does not reveal detail that the instrument cannot separate. Because of diffraction, two points closer than a minimum distance $d$ blur into one. For a microscope objective accepting a cone of half-angle β in a medium of index n:
$$d = \dfrac{\lambda}{2n\sin\beta},\qquad \text{resolving power} = \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{2n\sin\beta}{\lambda}$$
bullets: n sin β is the **numerical aperture** of the objective.
Formula only: the derivation is not required.

slides.narration: Light spreads slightly as it passes through the objective, so the image of a point is a tiny blurred disc. If two points are too close, their discs overlap and they look like one. The smallest separation that can still be told apart is the wavelength divided by twice n sine beta, where beta is the half-angle of the cone of light the objective accepts. Its reciprocal is the resolving power.

slides.heading: Increasing the resolving power
slides.body_md: To resolve finer detail, make d smaller:
bullets: **Shorter wavelength:** blue or violet light, or ultraviolet with a camera; electron microscopes use electrons of very short de Broglie wavelength.
**Higher n:** fill the gap between the slide and the objective with cedar-wood or synthetic oil (**oil immersion**, n ≈ 1.5).
**Larger β:** an objective of wide aperture very close to the object.
A stronger eyepiece only enlarges the blur (**empty magnification**).

visual.alt: Graph of the smallest separation a microscope can resolve against the numerical aperture n sine beta, for green light of 550 nanometres and violet light of 400 nanometres: the separation falls as the numerical aperture grows, and is always smaller for the shorter wavelength; a dry objective cannot exceed a numerical aperture of 1, while oil immersion goes beyond it
visual.caption: d = λ/(2 n sin β): larger numerical aperture and shorter wavelength resolve finer detail.

slides.narration: The formula shows three ways to resolve finer detail. Use a shorter wavelength, such as blue light, ultraviolet with a camera, or the very short wavelengths of an electron microscope. Raise the refractive index by placing a drop of oil between the slide and the objective. Or accept a wider cone of light. A stronger eyepiece does not help: it only enlarges the blur.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: oil immersion
slides.body_md: An objective accepts a cone with sin β = 0.90. Using green light of wavelength 550 nm, find the smallest separation it resolves (a) in air, (b) with oil of refractive index 1.52. Find the resolving power in air.
bullets: (a) $d = \dfrac{550}{2 \times 1 \times 0.90} = 306$ nm.
(b) Numerical aperture $1.52 \times 0.90 = 1.368$: $d = \dfrac{550}{2 \times 1.368} = 201$ nm, finer by the factor 1.52.
Resolving power in air $= \dfrac{1}{d} = 3.27 \times 10^{6}$ m⁻¹.

slides.narration: In air the smallest separation is five hundred and fifty divided by twice nought point nine, about three hundred and six nanometres. With oil of index one point five two, the numerical aperture rises to about one point three seven and the smallest separation falls to about two hundred and one nanometres: the oil improves the resolving power by the factor one point five two.

slides.heading: Uses, advantages and drawbacks
slides.body_md: Each instrument suits a job:
bullets: Microscopes: biology, medicine, metallurgy, forensic work. Telescopes: astronomy, navigation, surveying (with erecting systems).

rows: Watch and jewellery repair, reading fine print, examining leaves and insects
Magnifying power only up to about 10
Cells, bacteria, blood smears, metal grains
Inverted image, small field, needs bright light; detail limited by resolving power
Moon and planets, small observatories, finder scopes
Sealed tube, no central obstruction, little upkeep
Chromatic aberration; large lenses sag, absorb light and are costly; long tube; inverted image
Large research telescopes, faint galaxies, photography
No chromatic aberration, very large apertures, short tube
Secondary blocks some light; mirror needs re-coating and alignment

visual.alt: Table of the uses, advantages and drawbacks of the simple microscope, the compound microscope, the refracting telescope and the reflecting telescope

slides.narration: Each instrument has its place. A simple magnifier is cheap and gives an erect image, but only up to about ten times. A compound microscope reaches hundreds of times, with an inverted image and a small field, and its detail is limited by resolving power. Refracting telescopes are simple and sealed but suffer colour fringes and cannot be made very large. Reflecting telescopes dominate research astronomy.

slides.narration: To sum up: a refracting telescope in normal adjustment magnifies f o over f e, and a little more with the image at the near point. Large telescopes use a concave primary and a convex secondary, free of colour fringes. And the finest detail a microscope can show depends on the wavelength, the refractive index of the medium and the cone of light, not on the eyepiece.

sections.heading: 1. Magnifying power and the simple microscope
sections.body_md:
- **Magnifying power** $M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}$: β is the angle subtended at the eye by the final image; α is the angle subtended by the object without the instrument (for a microscope, the object held at the near point, D = 25 cm). Small angles: angle = height/distance.
- **Simple microscope** (a convex lens held close to the eye, object inside F): virtual, erect, enlarged image.
- **Image at D (derivation):** v = −D in $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{|u|} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{D}$. With the eye at the lens, β = h/|u| and α = h/D, so $M = \dfrac{D}{|u|} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}$ (equal to the linear magnification v/u).
- **Image at infinity (derivation):** object at F, rays leave parallel; β = h/f, α = h/D, so $M = \dfrac{D}{f}$ (relaxed eye; one less than at D).
- A shorter focal length magnifies more, but very short lenses are tiny, need the object almost touching them and suffer aberrations: in practice M up to about 10.

key_terms.definition_md: The least distance of distinct vision, about 25 cm for a normal eye: the closest an object can be seen sharply.
The ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle subtended by the object viewed without the instrument.

sections.heading: 2. The compound microscope
sections.body_md:
- **Construction:** objective of very short focal length f_o and small aperture; eyepiece of short focal length f_e. Object just beyond F_o; the objective forms a real, inverted, enlarged image A′B′ just inside F_e; the eyepiece forms the final virtual image A″B″ (inverted relative to the object, greatly enlarged).
- **Final image at D (derivation):** β = h′/|u_e| (A″B″ subtends the same angle as A′B′ at the eye), α = h/D, so $M = \dfrac{h'}{h}\cdot\dfrac{D}{|u_e|} = m_o m_e$ with $m_o = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}$ and $m_e = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}$: $M = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$. Lens separation $v_o + |u_e|$.
- **Approximation:** $\dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|} = \dfrac{v_o}{f_o} - 1 \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}$ (object near F_o, A′B′ a distance L ≈ tube length from the objective).
- **Final image at infinity (expression only, derivation not required):** A′B′ at F_e; $M = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e} \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e}$; separation $v_o + f_e$.
- High M needs short f_o and short f_e; an object at 2F_o would give m_o = 1.

key_terms.definition_md: The lens nearer the object; in a microscope it has a very short focal length and forms a real, enlarged image.
The lens next to the eye; it acts as a simple microscope on the image formed by the objective.

sections.heading: 3. The refracting astronomical telescope
sections.body_md:
- **Construction:** objective of long focal length f_o and large aperture (collects light, forms a real image of the distant object at F_o); eyepiece of short focal length f_e. α is the angle the object subtends where it is.
- **Normal adjustment (derivation):** the image I (height h) lies at F_o and at F_e. α = h/f_o, β = h/f_e, so $M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$; length $L = f_o + f_e$; final image at infinity, inverted.
- **Final image at D (derivation):** I lies |u_e| from the eyepiece with $\dfrac{1}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{1}{f_e} + \dfrac{1}{D}$; β = h/|u_e|, α = h/f_o, so $M = \dfrac{f_o}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_e}{D}\right)$; length $f_o + |u_e|$ (slightly shorter).
- The objective’s diameter does not change M; the light collected grows with its area (brighter images, finer detail). Terrestrial telescopes add an erecting system.

sections.heading: 4. Reflecting telescopes
sections.body_md:
- **Cassegrain type:** a large concave paraboloidal primary mirror reflects the light towards its focus; a small convex secondary mirror inside that focus reflects it back through a hole in the primary to a focus behind it, viewed with an eyepiece (or recorded by a camera). Image at infinity: $M = \dfrac{F}{f_e}$, F being the focal length of the mirror system (the convex secondary makes F several times the primary’s focal length while the tube stays short).
- **Advantages over refractors:** no chromatic aberration (reflection does not depend on n); no spherical aberration with a paraboloid; a mirror is supported over its whole back, so very large apertures are possible (a lens sags); only one surface to figure and no light absorbed in glass, so cheaper and brighter; greater light-gathering and resolving power; short tube.
- **Drawbacks:** the secondary blocks a little light (the image stays complete, slightly dimmer); mirrors need re-coating and careful alignment.

key_terms.definition_md: Coloured fringes in an image because a lens focuses different colours at different distances, its refractive index depending on wavelength.
Blurring because rays far from the axis are focused at a different point from paraxial rays.

sections.heading: 5. Resolving power; uses, advantages and drawbacks
sections.body_md:
- **Resolving power of a microscope** (formula only): two points closer than $d = \dfrac{\lambda}{2n\sin\beta}$ cannot be seen as separate; resolving power $= \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{2n\sin\beta}{\lambda}$. β is the half-angle of the cone of light from the object accepted by the objective; n sin β is the **numerical aperture**.
- **Factors:** wavelength (shorter is better), refractive index of the medium between object and objective, and β. **To increase it:** blue, violet or ultraviolet light (or electrons in an electron microscope); oil immersion (n ≈ 1.5); a wide-aperture objective close to the object. A stronger eyepiece gives only empty magnification.
- **Uses:** simple microscope — watch and jewellery repair, reading fine print, field biology; compound microscope — cells, bacteria, blood tests, metallurgy, forensic work; telescopes — astronomy, navigation, surveying.
- **Advantages and drawbacks:** simple microscope cheap and erect but M ≤ about 10; compound microscope high M but inverted image, small field, needs strong light; refractors sealed and simple but chromatic aberration and size limits; reflectors large and colour-free but a central obstruction and upkeep.

key_terms.definition_md: The reciprocal of the smallest separation between two points that an instrument can show as separate.
The product n sin β for a microscope objective, where β is the half-angle of the accepted cone of light and n the index of the medium in front of the objective.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Always say what α and β are; D = 25 cm; magnifying powers are quoted as magnitudes.
- Microscopes: simple 1 + D/f (D) and D/f (infinity); compound (v_o/|u_o|)(1 + D/f_e) at D, (v_o/|u_o|)(D/f_e) at infinity (expression only).
- Telescopes: f_o/f_e with L = f_o + f_e; (f_o/f_e)(1 + f_e/D) at D.
- Reflectors: concave primary, convex secondary, hole; no chromatic aberration. Resolving power 2n sin β/λ, not changed by the eyepiece.

cards.front_md: Magnifying power of an optical instrument?
cards.back_md: M = β/α: angle of the final image at the eye ÷ angle of the object without the instrument.

cards.front_md: Least distance of distinct vision used in ISC problems?
cards.back_md: D = 25 cm (the near point of a normal eye).

cards.front_md: Simple microscope, image at D: M?
cards.back_md: $1 + \dfrac{D}{f}$.

cards.front_md: Simple microscope, image at infinity: M?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{D}{f}$; object at the focus.

cards.front_md: Where is the object for a simple microscope with the image at D?
cards.back_md: Inside F, with 1/|u| = 1/f + 1/D.

cards.front_md: Lens of f = 12.5 cm as a magnifier: M at D and at infinity?
cards.back_md: 3 and 2.

cards.front_md: Why is a simple microscope limited to about 10×?
cards.back_md: Very short focal lengths need tiny, strongly curved lenses: small field and large aberrations.

cards.front_md: Image formed by the objective of a compound microscope?
cards.back_md: Real, inverted, enlarged, just inside the focus of the eyepiece (image at D).

cards.front_md: Compound microscope, final image at D: M?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$.

cards.front_md: Compound microscope, final image at infinity: M?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e}$ (expression only).

cards.front_md: Approximate M of a compound microscope?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$, L ≈ tube length.

cards.front_md: Exact objective magnification from v_o and f_o?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|} = \dfrac{v_o}{f_o} - 1$.

cards.front_md: Final image of a compound microscope relative to the object?
cards.back_md: Virtual, inverted, greatly enlarged.

cards.front_md: Lens separation in a compound microscope, image at infinity?
cards.back_md: v_o + f_e.

cards.front_md: Objective and eyepiece focal lengths for a powerful microscope?
cards.back_md: Both short (objective very short).

cards.front_md: Telescope in normal adjustment: M and length?
cards.back_md: M = f_o/f_e; L = f_o + f_e.

cards.front_md: Telescope with the final image at D: M?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_e}{D}\right)$.

cards.front_md: What is normal adjustment?
cards.back_md: Final image at infinity: the objective’s image lies at the focus of the eyepiece.

cards.front_md: Why a large aperture for a telescope objective?
cards.back_md: More light (∝ area) and finer detail; M is unchanged.

cards.front_md: fo = 80 cm, fe = 8.0 cm: M normal and at D?
Mirrors of a Cassegrain telescope?
cards.back_md: Concave paraboloidal primary with a central hole; small convex secondary.

cards.front_md: Why no chromatic aberration in a mirror?
cards.back_md: Reflection does not depend on refractive index, so all colours focus together.

cards.front_md: Why paraboloidal, not spherical, primary mirrors?
cards.back_md: A paraboloid brings all parallel rays to one focus: no spherical aberration.

cards.front_md: Why can mirrors be made larger than lenses?
cards.back_md: A mirror is supported over its whole back; a lens only at its rim, so it sags.

cards.front_md: Magnifying power of a reflecting telescope, image at infinity?
cards.back_md: M = F/f_e, F = focal length of the mirror system.

cards.front_md: Resolving power of a microscope?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{2n\sin\beta}{\lambda}$ = 1/d.

cards.front_md: What is the numerical aperture?
cards.back_md: n sin β of the objective.

cards.front_md: Three ways to raise a microscope’s resolving power?
cards.back_md: Shorter wavelength; oil immersion (higher n); wider cone (larger β).

cards.front_md: Does a stronger eyepiece improve resolution?
cards.back_md: No: empty magnification; it only enlarges the blur.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: α for a telescope?
cards.back_md: The angle subtended by the object where it is (h/f_o), not at D.

questions.stem_md: A convex lens of focal length f is used as a magnifying glass, held close to the eye, with the final image adjusted to the least distance of distinct vision D. Its magnifying power is

options.text_md: D/f
1 + D/f
D/f − 1
1 + f/D

questions.solution_md: With v = −D, 1/|u| = 1/f + 1/D, and M = β/α = (h/|u|)/(h/D) = D/|u| = 1 + D/f. D/f is the value for the image at infinity — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A hand lens gives a magnifying power of 4.5 when the image of a postage stamp is formed at the near point (25 cm). When the stamp is moved so that the image is at infinity, the magnifying power becomes
questions.solution_md: $1 + \dfrac{D}{f} = 4.5$ gives $\dfrac{D}{f} = 3.5$ (so $f = 7.14$ cm). With the image at infinity $M = \dfrac{D}{f} = 3.5$: always exactly one less — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A gem-tester’s loupe is a single convex lens of power +32 D. Find its magnifying power when it is used with a relaxed eye (final image at infinity).
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{32}$ m $= 3.125$ cm. Image at infinity: $M = \dfrac{D}{f} = \dfrac{25}{3.125} = 8.0$.

questions.stem_md: A biology student studies the veins of a leaf through a hand lens of focal length 7.5 cm held close to her eye, with the image formed at 25 cm. The leaf must be held at a distance from the lens of about

options.text_md: 7.5 cm
5.8 cm
3.3 cm

questions.solution_md: $v = -25$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{f} = -\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{7.5}$, so $|u| = 5.77$ cm — option (b). At 7.5 cm (the focus) the image would be at infinity; 10.7 cm comes from subtracting the reciprocals; 3.3 is D/f, the magnifying power at infinity.

questions.stem_md: A stamp collector uses a convex lens of focal length 4.0 cm held close to the eye, and adjusts the stamp until its image is at the near point, 25 cm away. How far from the lens is the stamp? Answer in cm (3 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: v = −25 cm in the lens formula: 1/|u| = 1/4.0 + 1/25

questions.stem_md: A naturalist examines an insect’s wing through a hand lens of focal length 10 cm with a relaxed eye, the final image being at infinity. The magnifying power is ___.
questions.solution_md: Image at infinity: $M = \dfrac{D}{f} = \dfrac{25}{10} = 2.5$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If a magnifying glass is first used with the object at its focus and then with the object moved slightly closer so that the image comes in to the near point, its magnifying power rises by exactly one.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. With the object at the focus, M = D/f (image at infinity); with the image at the near point, M = 1 + D/f. The difference is exactly 1, whatever the lens.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For a magnifying glass held close to the eye with the image at the near point, the magnifying power is equal to the linear magnification v/u of the image.

**Reason (R):** With the eye at the lens, an image of height h′ at distance D subtends the angle h′/D, while the object held at D without the lens subtends h/D.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: M = β/α = (h′/D)/(h/D) = h′/h, which is the linear magnification v/u (here D/|u| = 1 + D/f) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two people use the same magnifying glass of focal length 8.0 cm, each adjusting the image to their own near point: one has a near point of 25 cm, the other (who is long-sighted) of 50 cm. Find the magnifying power each obtains, and explain why the long-sighted person gains more from the lens.

answer.model_answer_md: $M = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}$ with each person’s own D: $1 + \dfrac{25}{8.0} = 4.13$ and $1 + \dfrac{50}{8.0} = 7.25$. M compares with the best unaided view, α = h/D. The long-sighted person must hold the object twice as far away to see it clearly, so α is half as large, while with the lens both view it from only about 6–7 cm, so β is nearly the same: the ratio β/α is larger for the long-sighted person.

questions.solution_md: M = 1 + D/f with D = 25 cm and 50 cm.

marking_scheme.step: Larger D makes the unaided angle α smaller, so the gain is larger

questions.stem_md: A student claims that a single glass bead lens of focal length 2.0 mm would make a simple microscope with a magnifying power of more than 100, and that compound microscopes are therefore unnecessary. Evaluate the claim.

answer.model_answer_md: On paper the claim holds: $M = 1 + \dfrac{25}{0.20} = 126$. In practice it is **not** a good replacement: the bead is about the size of the focal length, so the object must be held about 2 mm from it and the eye pressed against it; the field of view is tiny and so little light is collected; and a strongly curved lens gives large spherical and chromatic aberration. A compound microscope reaches high M with comfortable distances and corrected lenses.

questions.solution_md: M = 1 + D/f is large, but distances, field and aberrations make it impractical.

marking_scheme.step: Impractical: object ~2 mm away, tiny field, aberrations; compound microscope needed

questions.stem_md: Define the magnifying power of a simple microscope. Derive an expression for it (a) when the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision D, (b) when the final image is at infinity.

answer.model_answer_md:
Magnifying power $M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}$: the angle subtended at the eye by the image ÷ the angle subtended by the object placed at D and viewed directly ($\alpha = h/D$). The eye is close to the lens.
(a) The object, of height h, is inside F at distance |u|; the virtual image is at $v = -D$. $\beta = \dfrac{h}{|u|}$, so $M = \dfrac{D}{|u|}$. From $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$: $-\dfrac{1}{D} + \dfrac{1}{|u|} = \dfrac{1}{f}$, so $\dfrac{D}{|u|} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}$, i.e. $M = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}$.
(b) The object is at F; the rays leave parallel and $\beta = \dfrac{h}{f}$, so $M = \dfrac{D}{f}$.

questions.solution_md: β/α with α = h/D; lens formula with v = −D; object at F for (b).

marking_scheme.step: Definition with α for the object at D

questions.stem_md: (a) With the help of a ray diagram (described in words), derive the magnifying power of a simple microscope when the image is formed at the near point, and state how it changes when the image is formed at infinity. [3] (b) An engraver uses a lens of power +12 D as a simple microscope. (i) Find the magnifying power with the image at the near point and at infinity. [1] (ii) How far from the lens must the work be held in the first case? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The object AB, of height h, is placed inside the focus F of a convex lens held close to the eye. Rays from A — one parallel to the axis (refracted through F₂) and one through the optical centre (undeviated) — diverge after the lens; traced back, they meet at A′, giving a virtual, erect, enlarged image A′B′ at the near point, $v = -D$.
$\beta = \dfrac{h}{|u|}$ (angle of the image at the eye) and $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{D}$ (object held at D without the lens), so $M = \dfrac{D}{|u|}$. The lens formula with $v = -D$ gives $\dfrac{1}{|u|} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{D}$, so $M = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}$. With the object at F the image is at infinity and $M = \dfrac{D}{f}$, one less.

(b)(i) $f = \dfrac{1}{12}$ m $= 8.33$ cm: $M = 1 + 25 \times 0.12 = 4$ at the near point, $M = 3$ at infinity.
(ii) $\dfrac{1}{|u|} = 0.12 + 0.04 = 0.16$ cm⁻¹, so $|u| = 6.25$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Ray diagram, β/α, lens formula with v = −D; then P → f.

marking_scheme.step: Ray diagram described: object inside F, virtual erect image at D
M = 1 + D/f; D/f for the image at infinity

questions.stem_md: A watch repairer wants a single-lens magnifier that gives a magnifying power of 12.5 when used with a relaxed eye. What focal length must the lens have? Answer in cm.
questions.solution_md: Image at infinity: $M = \dfrac{D}{f}$, so $f = \dfrac{25}{12.5} = 2.0$ cm (power +50 D).

questions.stem_md: In a compound microscope adjusted so that the final image is at the near point, the image formed by the objective is

options.text_md: real, inverted and enlarged, lying just inside the focus of the eyepiece
virtual, erect and enlarged, lying just outside the focus of the eyepiece
real, erect and diminished, lying at the focus of the objective
real, inverted and enlarged, lying beyond twice the focal length of the eyepiece

questions.solution_md: The object is just beyond F_o, so the objective forms a real, inverted, enlarged image. The eyepiece must form a virtual magnified image of it, so it lies inside F_e — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A pathology student views a stained cell through a compound microscope with the final image at the near point. Compared with the cell itself, the final image is

options.text_md: virtual, inverted and greatly enlarged
real, inverted and greatly enlarged
virtual, erect and greatly enlarged
real, erect and slightly enlarged

questions.solution_md: The objective forms a real, inverted image; the eyepiece, used as a magnifier, forms a virtual image of it without turning it again. So the final image is virtual and inverted relative to the cell, and enlarged by m_o × m_e — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A microscope has an objective of focal length 0.80 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm. A specimen is 0.90 cm in front of the objective, and the final image is formed 25 cm from the eyepiece. Find the magnifying power.

In a student’s microscope the objective has a focal length of 1.2 cm and the eyepiece 3.0 cm. A small seed is 1.5 cm from the objective, and the microscope is focused so that the final image is at the near point. Find the distance between the two lenses, in cm (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Objective: $\dfrac{1}{v_o} = \dfrac{1}{1.2} - \dfrac{1}{1.5} = \dfrac{1}{6.0}$, $v_o = 6.0$ cm. Eyepiece, image at 25 cm: $\dfrac{1}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{1}{3.0} + \dfrac{1}{25}$, $|u_e| = 2.68$ cm. Separation $= 6.0 + 2.68 = 8.68$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The objective of a microscope forms an image 30 times as large as the specimen, and the eyepiece has a focal length of 2.0 cm. The microscope is set for a relaxed eye, with the final image at infinity. Its magnifying power is
questions.solution_md: Final image at infinity: $M = m_o \cdot \dfrac{D}{f_e} = 30 \times \dfrac{25}{2.0} = 375$ — option (c). 405 uses $1 + D/f_e$ (image at D); 60 multiplies by $f_e$; 15 divides by it.

questions.stem_md: A microscope has an objective of focal length 1.0 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm. An object is 1.1 cm from the objective, and the eyepiece is set so that the final image is at infinity. Using the expression for this setting, find the magnifying power.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v_o} = \dfrac{1}{1.0} - \dfrac{1}{1.1}$, so $v_o = 11$ cm and $m_o = \dfrac{11}{1.1} = 10$. $M = m_o \dfrac{D}{f_e} = 10 \times \dfrac{25}{4.0} = 62.5$ (lenses $11 + 4.0 = 15$ cm apart).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a compound microscope, the eyepiece forms a real image of the objective’s image, and the eye looks at this real image.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The objective’s image lies inside the focus of the eyepiece (or at it), so the eyepiece acts as a magnifying glass and forms a virtual image (at D or at infinity). The only real image is the one formed by the objective.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The final image seen in a compound microscope is inverted with respect to the object.

**Reason (R):** The eyepiece of a compound microscope inverts the image formed by the objective.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the eyepiece forms a virtual, erect image of the objective’s image (like a magnifying glass). The inversion is done by the objective, which forms a real, inverted image — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A microscope with an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm is focused with the final image at the near point (25 cm). To view with a relaxed eye (final image at infinity) without moving the specimen or the objective, the eyepiece must be moved

options.text_md: about 0.55 cm towards the objective
about 4.0 cm away from the objective
about 0.55 cm away from the objective
about 3.45 cm towards the objective

questions.solution_md: For the image at D the objective’s image is $|u_e| = \dfrac{1}{1/4.0 + 1/25} = 3.45$ cm from the eyepiece; for the image at infinity it must be at the focus, 4.0 cm away. The eyepiece moves out by $4.0 - 3.45 = 0.55$ cm, away from the objective — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Show that the linear magnification of the objective of a microscope can be written as v_o/f_o − 1. An objective of focal length 0.40 cm forms its image 20 cm away: compare its exact magnification with the estimate L/f_o, taking L = 20 cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
From $\dfrac{1}{v_o} - \dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{f_o}$, multiply by $v_o$: $1 - \dfrac{v_o}{u_o} = \dfrac{v_o}{f_o}$, so $\dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|} = \dfrac{v_o}{f_o} - 1$.
Here $\dfrac{20}{0.40} - 1 = 49$, against the estimate $\dfrac{L}{f_o} = 50$: only 2% high, because $v_o \gg f_o$.

questions.solution_md: Multiply the lens formula by v_o.

marking_scheme.step: m_o = v_o/f_o − 1 from the lens formula

questions.stem_md: A student sets up a compound microscope with the specimen at twice the focal length of the objective, “so that the objective’s image is sharp and well placed”. Explain, using the objective’s magnification, why this is a poor choice and where the specimen should be.

answer.model_answer_md: At $u_o = -2f_o$ the objective forms its image at $v_o = 2f_o$, so $m_o = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|} = 1$: the objective does not magnify at all, and the whole magnifying power comes from the eyepiece. The specimen should be **just beyond $F_o$**, so that $v_o$ is large compared with $|u_o|$ and the objective gives a large real image (e.g. $m_o \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}$).

questions.solution_md: m_o = 1 at 2F_o.

marking_scheme.step: At 2F_o, v_o = 2f_o and m_o = 1: no magnification from the objective
Specimen just beyond F_o makes v_o ≫ |u_o|

questions.stem_md: Describe, with a labelled ray diagram (in words), how a compound microscope forms the final image at the least distance of distinct vision, and derive an expression for its magnifying power in this adjustment.

answer.model_answer_md:
The object AB is placed just beyond the focus $F_o$ of the objective, which forms a real, inverted, enlarged image A′B′ (height $h'$) inside the focus $F_e$ of the eyepiece. The eyepiece acts as a simple microscope and forms a virtual image A″B″ at D.
A″B″ subtends at the eye the same angle as A′B′: $\beta = \dfrac{h'}{|u_e|}$. The object at D unaided subtends $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{D}$. So $M = \dfrac{h'}{h}\cdot\dfrac{D}{|u_e|}$.
$\dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}$ and, with $v = -D$ for the eyepiece, $\dfrac{D}{|u_e|} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}$: $M = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right) \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$.

questions.solution_md: m_o × m_e with m_e = 1 + D/f_e.

marking_scheme.step: Ray diagram described: A′B′ real, inverted, inside F_e; A″B″ virtual at D

questions.stem_md: A microscope is to give a magnifying power of 135 with the final image at the near point, using an eyepiece of focal length 2.0 cm and an objective of focal length 1.5 cm. Find how far from the objective the specimen must be, and the distance between the two lenses.

answer.model_answer_md:
Eyepiece: $m_e = 1 + \dfrac{25}{2.0} = 13.5$, so the objective must give $m_o = \dfrac{135}{13.5} = 10$.
With $v_o = m_o|u_o|$ in the lens formula: $v_o = f_o(1 + m_o) = 1.5 \times 11 = 16.5$ cm and $|u_o| = \dfrac{16.5}{10} = 1.65$ cm.
Eyepiece object distance: $\dfrac{1}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{1}{2.0} + \dfrac{1}{25}$, $|u_e| = 1.85$ cm. Separation $= 16.5 + 1.85 = 18.35$ cm.

questions.solution_md: m_o = M/m_e; v_o = f_o(1 + m_o); separation v_o + |u_e|.

questions.stem_md: A microscope has an objective of focal length 0.75 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 2.0 cm, with a specimen 0.80 cm from the objective. Find the magnifying power and the separation of the lenses (a) with the final image at the near point, (b) with the final image at infinity.

answer.model_answer_md:
Objective: $\dfrac{1}{v_o} = \dfrac{1}{0.75} - \dfrac{1}{0.80}$, $v_o = 12.0$ cm, $m_o = \dfrac{12}{0.80} = 15$.
(a) $M = 15\left(1 + \dfrac{25}{2.0}\right) = 202.5$; $|u_e| = 1.85$ cm, so the lenses are $13.85$ cm apart.
(b) $M = 15 \times \dfrac{25}{2.0} = 187.5$; the objective’s image is at $F_e$, so the lenses are $12 + 2.0 = 14.0$ cm apart.

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe in words) a labelled ray diagram of a compound microscope with the final image at the least distance of distinct vision D, and derive the expression for its magnifying power in this adjustment. [3] (b) In such a microscope the objective has a focal length of 1.25 cm and the eyepiece 3.0 cm; a specimen is placed 1.5 cm from the objective. Find the magnifying power with the final image at D and the distance between the lenses. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Object AB just beyond $F_o$; objective forms a real, inverted, enlarged image A′B′ (height $h'$) just inside $F_e$; the eyepiece forms the virtual, enlarged final image A″B″ at D (inverted relative to AB). Rays from A: one parallel to the axis, refracted through $F_o'$ to A′; one through the objective’s centre to A′; from A′ they diverge after the eyepiece, as if from A″.
$\beta = \dfrac{h'}{|u_e|}$, $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{D}$, so $M = \dfrac{h'}{h}\cdot\dfrac{D}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$, using $\dfrac{1}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{1}{f_e} + \dfrac{1}{D}$ for the eyepiece.

(b) $\dfrac{1}{v_o} = \dfrac{1}{1.25} - \dfrac{1}{1.5} = \dfrac{2}{15}$, $v_o = 7.5$ cm, $m_o = 5$; $M = 5\left(1 + \dfrac{25}{3.0}\right) = 46.7$. $|u_e| = 2.68$ cm, so the lenses are $10.18$ cm apart.

questions.solution_md: Ray diagram; M = m_o m_e; then numbers.

marking_scheme.step: Ray diagram described with A′B′ inside F_e and A″B″ at D

questions.stem_md: Estimate the magnifying power of a microscope, set for a relaxed eye, whose objective (focal length 0.45 cm) forms its image 18 cm away and whose eyepiece has a focal length of 5.0 cm. Use the approximation L/f_o for the objective.
questions.solution_md: $M \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e} = \dfrac{18}{0.45} \times \dfrac{25}{5.0} = 40 \times 5 = 200$ (exactly, $m_o = 39$ and $M = 195$).

questions.stem_md: An observer adjusts an astronomical telescope so that she can view the Moon with a relaxed eye (normal adjustment). The image of the Moon formed by the objective then lies

options.text_md: at the near point of the observer’s eye
at the focus of the objective, which coincides with the focus of the eyepiece
midway between the objective and the eyepiece
at twice the focal length of the eyepiece from it

questions.solution_md: Light from the distant Moon is focused in the focal plane of the objective. For the rays to leave the eyepiece parallel (final image at infinity), that image must also be at the focus of the eyepiece, so the lenses are f_o + f_e apart — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A refracting telescope built with an objective of focal length 90 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 3.6 cm is set in normal adjustment. The lenses are then ___ cm apart.
questions.solution_md: In normal adjustment L = f_o + f_e = 90 + 3.6 = **93.6** cm.

questions.stem_md: Jupiter subtends an angle of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ rad at the Earth. What angle does its final image subtend at the eye when it is viewed through a telescope in normal adjustment, with an objective of focal length 90 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 3.6 cm? Answer in rad.
questions.solution_md: $M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = \dfrac{90}{3.6} = 25$, and $\beta = M\alpha = 25 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-4} = 0.0050$ rad.

questions.stem_md: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 140 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 3.5 cm. Find its magnifying power when it is adjusted so that the final image is at the near point (25 cm).
questions.solution_md: $M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_e}{D}\right) = 40 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{3.5}{25}\right) = 40 \times 1.14 = 45.6$.

questions.stem_md: An astronomical telescope with an objective of focal length 140 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 3.5 cm is first in normal adjustment. By how much must the eyepiece be moved, and in which direction, to bring the final image to the near point, 25 cm from the eye? Give the distance in cm.
questions.solution_md: Normal adjustment: the objective’s image is 3.5 cm from the eyepiece. For the image at D: $\dfrac{1}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{1}{3.5} + \dfrac{1}{25}$, so $|u_e| = 3.07$ cm. The eyepiece moves $3.5 - 3.07 = 0.43$ cm **towards the objective** (tube $143.1$ cm instead of 143.5 cm).

marking_scheme.step: |u_e| = 3.07 cm for the image at D

questions.stem_md: An astronomical telescope is changed from normal adjustment to the setting in which the final image is at the near point. Compared with normal adjustment, the magnifying power and the distance between the lenses

options.text_md: decrease and increase respectively
both increase
both stay the same
increase and decrease respectively

questions.solution_md: M changes from f_o/f_e to (f_o/f_e)(1 + f_e/D), which is larger; the objective’s image must now lie inside the focus of the eyepiece, so the eyepiece moves in and L = f_o + |u_e| is less than f_o + f_e — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a distant water tank on a hill is viewed through an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment, it appears upside down.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The objective forms a real, inverted image of the distant object; the eyepiece magnifies it without inverting it again, so the final image is inverted. (Terrestrial telescopes add an erecting lens or prisms.)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In normal adjustment the distance between the objective and the eyepiece of an astronomical telescope equals the sum of their focal lengths.

**Reason (R):** The final image formed by an astronomical telescope is inverted.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A. A follows because the image formed by the objective lies at the focus of both lenses; the inversion (R) is due to the objective forming a real image — option (b).

questions.stem_md: With the help of a ray diagram (described in words), derive an expression for the magnifying power of a refracting astronomical telescope in normal adjustment. State the distance between the lenses in this adjustment.

answer.model_answer_md:
Parallel rays from the top of a distant object reach the objective at a small angle α to the axis. The objective brings them to a point A′ in its focal plane, forming a real, inverted image A′B′ of height h at $F_o$: $\alpha \approx \dfrac{h}{f_o}$ (from the ray through the objective’s centre).
In normal adjustment A′B′ is also at the focus of the eyepiece, so the rays from A′ leave the eyepiece parallel, at angle β with $\beta \approx \dfrac{h}{f_e}$ (ray through the eyepiece’s centre); the final image is at infinity.
$M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$; the lenses are $f_o + f_e$ apart.

questions.solution_md: α = h/f_o, β = h/f_e.

marking_scheme.step: Ray diagram: image at the common focus; rays leave parallel

questions.stem_md: A small telescope has an objective of focal length 60 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 2.0 cm. Find its magnifying power and the separation of the lenses (a) in normal adjustment, (b) with the final image at the near point.
questions.solution_md: f_o/f_e and f_o + f_e; then (1 + f_e/D) and f_o + |u_e|.

questions.stem_md: A telescope in normal adjustment must have a magnifying power of 35 and a tube length of 108 cm. Find the focal lengths of the objective and the eyepiece needed.

answer.model_answer_md: $f_o = 35 f_e$ and $f_o + f_e = 108$ cm, so $36 f_e = 108$: $f_e = 3.0$ cm and $f_o = 105$ cm.

questions.solution_md: f_o/f_e = 35 and f_o + f_e = 108.

questions.stem_md: The Moon subtends an angle of about 9.0 × 10⁻³ rad at the Earth. An observatory telescope has an objective of focal length 160 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm. Find the diameter of the Moon’s image formed by the objective, in cm.
questions.solution_md: The Moon is effectively at infinity, so its image is in the focal plane of the objective: diameter $= f_o\alpha = 160 \times 9.0 \times 10^{-3} = 1.44$ cm. (Viewed in normal adjustment it subtends $40 \times 9.0 \times 10^{-3} = 0.36$ rad at the eye.)

marking_scheme.step: Image in the focal plane: d = f_oα

questions.stem_md: Two telescopes have identical focal lengths (objective 120 cm, eyepiece 3.0 cm), but the objective of one is 6.0 cm in diameter and the other 12 cm. Compare their magnifying powers and the amounts of light they collect from a star, and say which would show a faint star cluster better.

answer.model_answer_md: Both have $M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = 40$: magnifying power does not depend on the aperture. The light collected is proportional to the **area** of the objective, so the 12 cm telescope collects $(12/6.0)^2 = 4$ times as much. It shows the faint cluster better: the images are brighter, and its wider aperture also resolves stars that are closer together.

questions.solution_md: M = f_o/f_e for both; light ∝ diameter².

marking_scheme.step: 4 times the light; the wider telescope is better for faint objects

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe in words) a labelled ray diagram of a refracting astronomical telescope with the final image formed at the least distance of distinct vision D, and derive the expression for its magnifying power. [3] (b) A telescope has an objective of focal length 75 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 2.5 cm. Find its magnifying power and length (i) in normal adjustment, (ii) with the final image at D. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Parallel rays from the top of a distant object, at angle α to the axis, are brought by the objective to A′ in its focal plane: a real, inverted image A′B′ of height h at $F_o$, so $\alpha = \dfrac{h}{f_o}$. The eyepiece is placed so that A′B′ lies just inside its focus, at $|u_e|$; it forms a virtual, magnified final image A″B″ at D, the emerging rays diverging as if from A″.
β, the angle subtended by A″B″ at the eye, equals that of A′B′: $\beta = \dfrac{h}{|u_e|}$. So $M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{f_o}{|u_e|}$. With $v = -D$: $\dfrac{1}{|u_e|} = \dfrac{1}{f_e} + \dfrac{1}{D}$, hence $M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_e}{D}\right)$.

(b)(i) $M = \dfrac{75}{2.5} = 30$, $L = 77.5$ cm. (ii) $M = 30 \times 1.1 = 33$; $|u_e| = \dfrac{1}{0.4 + 0.04} = 2.27$ cm, so $L = 77.27$ cm.

questions.solution_md: α = h/f_o, β = h/|u_e|; lens formula for the eyepiece with v = −D.

marking_scheme.step: Ray diagram described: A′B′ at F_o inside F_e; A″B″ at D

questions.stem_md: A college observatory has a refracting telescope whose objective has a focal length of 1.8 m. What focal length of eyepiece gives a magnifying power of 60 in normal adjustment? Answer in cm.
A bird-watcher wants to watch herons on a lake 300 m away. An astronomical telescope of suitable magnifying power is a poor choice mainly because

options.text_md: it cannot focus on objects nearer than a few kilometres
its magnifying power is less than 1 for nearby objects
it can be used only at night
it shows the birds upside down, unless an erecting lens or prisms are added

questions.solution_md: The objective forms a real, inverted image and the eyepiece does not turn it back, so terrestrial viewing needs an erecting system (a third lens, or prisms as in binoculars) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a Cassegrain reflecting telescope, the light reflected by the large primary mirror reaches the eyepiece after

options.text_md: reflection at a small plane mirror at 45°, which sends it out through the side of the tube
refraction through a convex lens placed at the focus of the primary
reflection at a small convex secondary mirror, which sends it back through a hole in the centre of the primary
reflection at a small concave mirror placed beyond the focus of the primary

questions.solution_md: In the Cassegrain design a convex secondary, placed inside the focus of the concave primary, reflects the converging light back along the axis through a central hole in the primary to a focus behind it. A 45° plane mirror sending light out sideways describes the Newtonian design — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A bright star seen through a large lens telescope shows faint coloured fringes, but the same star seen through a mirror telescope does not. This is because

options.text_md: a mirror collects more light than a lens of the same diameter
a mirror forms a virtual image, which has no colour
light travels faster in a mirror telescope tube than in glass
the angle of reflection does not depend on wavelength, while the refractive index of glass does

questions.solution_md: A lens focuses different colours at different distances because n of glass varies with wavelength (chromatic aberration). The law of reflection (i = r) involves no refractive index, so all colours reflected by a mirror meet at one focus — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A concave mirror of large aperture ground to a spherical shape brings all rays of a parallel beam to a single focus, which is why large telescope mirrors are made spherical.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. A spherical mirror of large aperture focuses rays far from the axis closer to the mirror than paraxial rays (spherical aberration). Telescope primaries are made paraboloidal, which brings all rays parallel to the axis to one point.

questions.stem_md: In a reflecting telescope the concave objective mirror has a radius of curvature of 4.0 m; a small plane mirror merely turns the converging beam aside to an eyepiece of focal length 2.5 cm. With the final image at infinity, the magnifying power is
questions.solution_md: The plane mirror does not change the focal length, so $f_o = \dfrac{R}{2} = 2.0$ m $= 200$ cm and $M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = \dfrac{200}{2.5} = 80$ — option (a). 160 uses R instead of R/2.

questions.stem_md: The mirror system of a Cassegrain telescope has an effective focal length of 3.2 m. Find the magnifying power with an eyepiece of focal length 2.0 cm, the final image being at infinity.

In a Cassegrain telescope the primary mirror has a focal length of 100 cm, and a convex secondary mirror of focal length 25 cm is placed 80 cm in front of it. Find where the light finally comes to a focus, the effective focal length of the mirror system, and the magnifying power with an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm (image at infinity).

answer.model_answer_md:
The primary alone would focus 100 cm from it, i.e. $100 - 80 = 20$ cm beyond the secondary: a **virtual object** for the secondary.
Mirror formula for the convex secondary ($f = -25$ cm, virtual object 20 cm behind it): $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{25} + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{100}$, so $v = 100$ cm in front of the secondary: the focus is $100 - 80 = 20$ cm **behind** the primary (through its hole).
The secondary magnifies $\dfrac{100}{20} = 5$ times, so $F = 5 \times 100 = 500$ cm and $M = \dfrac{500}{4.0} = 125$.

questions.solution_md: Virtual object for the secondary; F = f_primary × m_secondary.

marking_scheme.step: Virtual object 20 cm behind the secondary; v = 100 cm
Focus 20 cm behind the primary; F = 500 cm

questions.stem_md: A guide at an observatory tells visitors that India’s 3.6 m Devasthal telescope near Nainital could not sensibly have been built with a 3.6 m lens as its objective. Give two reasons from physics that support her.

answer.model_answer_md: Any two: (i) a lens can be held only at its rim, so a 3.6 m lens would **sag** under its own weight and distort the image, while a mirror is supported over its whole back; (ii) a lens shows **chromatic aberration**, a mirror does not; (iii) a lens needs a huge block of flawless, bubble-free glass and **two** accurately shaped surfaces, and the thick glass **absorbs** light; a mirror needs one coated surface.

questions.solution_md: Sag, chromatic aberration, flawless glass and absorption.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Because the small secondary mirror of a Cassegrain telescope blocks the centre of the incoming beam, the image of a planet seen through it has a dark hole in the middle.

**Reason (R):** The secondary mirror stops the central part of the light that would otherwise reach the primary mirror.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: every part of the remaining (ring-shaped) aperture receives light from every point of the planet and focuses it to the corresponding point of the image, so the image is complete — only slightly dimmer — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Someone sticks a small black paper disc over the centre of the objective of a telescope, covering one tenth of its area, and looks at the Moon. Compared with before, the image of the Moon is

options.text_md: missing its central part
smaller in size, but just as bright
complete and the same size, but slightly dimmer
unchanged in every way, because only the edges of a lens focus light

questions.solution_md: Each point of the Moon sends light through the whole uncovered aperture, and all of it is focused to the same image point. Blocking part of the aperture removes some light from every image point (about 10% less), but leaves the image whole and the magnifying power unchanged — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A school can afford either a refracting telescope with a 10 cm objective lens or a Cassegrain reflector with a 20 cm mirror, at the same price. Students mainly want to photograph faint nebulae. Evaluate the choice, giving one point against the option you recommend.

answer.model_answer_md: Recommend the **20 cm reflector**. (i) It collects $(20/10)^2 = 4$ times as much light, so faint nebulae show up in much shorter exposures, and its larger aperture resolves finer detail. (ii) A mirror has no chromatic aberration, so colour photographs are free of fringes, and the folded Cassegrain tube is short and easy to mount. **Against it:** the secondary mirror blocks some light and the mirrors need occasional re-alignment and re-coating, while a refractor’s sealed tube needs little upkeep.

questions.solution_md: Light ∝ diameter²; no chromatic aberration; upkeep against it.

marking_scheme.step: Reflector: 4 times the light (and better resolution)

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe in words) a labelled ray diagram of a Cassegrain reflecting telescope forming the final image at infinity. [2] (b) State two advantages of a reflecting telescope over a refracting one. [1] (c) A Cassegrain telescope has a mirror system of effective focal length 6.0 m. Find its magnifying power with eyepieces of focal lengths 2.0 cm and 5.0 cm, and say which eyepiece is better for viewing a large, faint galaxy. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Parallel rays from a distant object fall on a large **concave paraboloidal primary mirror** with a central hole. The converging reflected rays meet a small **convex secondary mirror** placed inside the primary’s focus, which reflects them back along the axis through the hole to a focus just behind the primary. An **eyepiece** placed so that this image is at its focus sends the rays out parallel: the final image is at infinity.

(b) Any two: no chromatic aberration; no spherical aberration with a paraboloidal mirror; a mirror can be supported from behind, so very large apertures are possible; one surface to figure, no light absorbed in glass; short tube.

(c) $M = \dfrac{F}{f_e}$: $\dfrac{600}{2.0} = 300$ and $\dfrac{600}{5.0} = 120$. The **5.0 cm** eyepiece is better for a large faint galaxy: the light is spread over a smaller image, so it looks brighter, and more of the galaxy fits in the field.

questions.solution_md: Concave primary, convex secondary, hole, eyepiece; M = F/f_e.

marking_scheme.step: Diagram: concave primary with hole, convex secondary
Rays to a focus behind the primary; eyepiece gives parallel rays
5.0 cm eyepiece: brighter image, wider field

questions.stem_md: A laboratory microscope just fails to separate two neighbouring granules in a cell lit with red light. The granules are most likely to be resolved by

options.text_md: lighting the specimen with violet light instead of red
fitting an eyepiece of shorter focal length
using a longer microscope tube
lighting the specimen with infrared radiation

questions.solution_md: d = λ/(2n sin β): a shorter wavelength makes the smallest resolvable separation smaller. A stronger eyepiece or a longer tube only increases the magnification of the blurred image; infrared has a longer wavelength — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A microscope objective has a numerical aperture n sin β of 0.80 and is used with blue light of wavelength 480 nm. Using d = λ/(2n sin β), find the smallest separation between two points of the specimen that it can resolve, in nm.
questions.solution_md: $d = \dfrac{480}{2 \times 0.80} = 300$ nm, i.e. $3.0 \times 10^{-7}$ m; resolving power $\dfrac{1}{d} = 3.33 \times 10^{6}$ m⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: An oil-immersion objective accepts light in a cone of half-angle 60°, the oil having a refractive index of 1.52. Using d = λ/(2n sin β), find the smallest separation it can resolve in orange light of wavelength 600 nm, in nm (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $n\sin\beta = 1.52 \times \sin 60° = 1.52 \times 0.866 = 1.316$; $d = \dfrac{600}{2 \times 1.316} = 228$ nm (without the oil it would be 346 nm).

questions.stem_md: The same microscope objective is used first with red light of wavelength 675 nm and then with blue light of wavelength 450 nm. Find the ratio of its resolving power in blue light to that in red light.
questions.solution_md: Resolving power $= \dfrac{2n\sin\beta}{\lambda} \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$, so the ratio is $\dfrac{675}{450} = 1.5$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Replacing the eyepiece of a microscope with one that doubles its magnifying power also doubles its resolving power.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Resolving power 2n sin β/λ depends on the wavelength, the medium and the objective’s cone of light, not on the eyepiece. A stronger eyepiece only enlarges the blurred image (empty magnification).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A microscope that records its images with an ultraviolet-sensitive camera can show finer detail of a specimen than the same microscope used with visible light.

**Reason (R):** The smallest separation a microscope can resolve is proportional to the wavelength of the light used.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: d = λ/(2n sin β), so ultraviolet light (shorter λ) gives a smaller d, i.e. finer detail — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For a microscope objective, the product of the refractive index of the medium in front of it and the sine of the half-angle of the cone of light it accepts, which fixes its resolving power, is called its ___.
questions.solution_md: The **numerical aperture**, n sin β; resolving power = 2n sin β/λ.

questions.stem_md: Write the expression for the resolving power of a compound microscope, naming each symbol. State two practical ways in which its resolving power can be increased.

answer.model_answer_md: Resolving power $= \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{2n\sin\beta}{\lambda}$, where d is the smallest resolvable separation, n the refractive index of the medium between the object and the objective, β the half-angle of the cone of light from the object accepted by the objective, and λ the wavelength. Ways (any two): use light of **shorter wavelength** (blue or ultraviolet); use **oil immersion** to raise n; use an objective of **wider aperture** close to the object (larger β).

questions.solution_md: RP = 2n sin β/λ.

questions.stem_md: A student wants to see two features of a bacterium that are 250 nm apart, using green light (550 nm) and a dry objective of numerical aperture 0.65. Finding them blurred together, she fits an eyepiece of much shorter focal length. Evaluate her approach, and suggest a better one supported by a calculation.

answer.model_answer_md:
With the dry objective $d = \dfrac{550}{2 \times 0.65} = 423$ nm, much more than 250 nm: the features cannot be resolved. A stronger eyepiece only enlarges the blurred image (**empty magnification**), so her approach fails.
Better: an **oil-immersion** objective, e.g. numerical aperture 1.25: $d = \dfrac{550}{2 \times 1.25} = 220$ nm < 250 nm, so the features are resolved. (Shorter wavelength light would also help.)

questions.solution_md: d = λ/(2 n sin β) for each objective.

questions.stem_md: Match each optical instrument in Column A with a drawback of it in Column B.

options.text_md: Simple microscope
Compound microscope
Large refracting telescope
Cassegrain reflecting telescope

match_right.text_md: Inverted image and a small field of view
Part of the incoming light blocked by the secondary mirror
Magnifying power limited to about ten by aberrations of short-focus lenses
Colour fringes, and an objective that sags because it can be held only at its rim

questions.solution_md: Simple microscope → limited magnifying power (1 → r); compound microscope → inverted image, small field (2 → p); large refractor → chromatic aberration and sagging lens (3 → s); Cassegrain → central obstruction by the secondary (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: Match each instrument setting in Column A with the distance between its objective and eyepiece in Column B (v_o is the image distance of a microscope objective; D = 25 cm).

options.text_md: Compound microscope, final image at infinity
Telescope in normal adjustment
Telescope, final image at D
Compound microscope, final image at D

questions.solution_md: Final image at infinity: the first image is at the eyepiece focus, so the distance is (image distance) + f_e: microscope v_o + f_e (1 → q), telescope f_o + f_e (2 → p). Final image at D: the first image is |u_e| = f_eD/(f_e + D) from the eyepiece: telescope (3 → s), microscope (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: (a) What is meant by the resolving power of a compound microscope? Write its expression and state the factors on which it depends. [2] (b) An objective accepts light in a cone of half-angle 64°. Find the smallest separation it can resolve in light of wavelength 450 nm (i) in air, (ii) with oil of refractive index 1.5 between the objective and the slide. [2] (c) Explain why fitting a stronger eyepiece does not let the microscope show finer detail. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Resolving power is the ability to show two close points of the object as separate; it is the reciprocal of the smallest separation d that can be resolved: $\dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{2n\sin\beta}{\lambda}$. It depends on the wavelength λ (shorter is better), the refractive index n of the medium between object and objective, and the half-angle β of the cone of light accepted by the objective.

(b) $\sin 64° = 0.899$. (i) $d = \dfrac{450}{2 \times 0.899} = 250$ nm. (ii) $d = \dfrac{450}{2 \times 1.5 \times 0.899} = 167$ nm.

(c) The eyepiece only magnifies the image formed by the objective. Detail that the objective has already blurred together cannot be separated by enlarging it: the result is a larger but equally blurred image (empty magnification).

questions.solution_md: RP = 2n sin β/λ; d in air and in oil.
